concepts.name: Running Python code
concepts.description: Writing instructions in a file or interpreter and getting Python to run them.

concepts.name: Variables and values
concepts.description: A variable is a name that stores a value, which can be changed by assigning a new one.

concepts.name: Basic data types
concepts.description: Values have types such as integers, floats, strings and booleans, which determine what operations work.

concepts.name: Expressions and operators
concepts.description: Combining values with operators like + - * / to produce a new value.

concepts.name: Strings
concepts.description: Text values written in quotes, which can be joined, sliced and measured.

concepts.name: Lists
concepts.description: Ordered collections of values that can be read by position and changed.

concepts.name: Conditionals
concepts.description: Using if, elif and else to run different code depending on whether a condition is true.

concepts.name: Loops
concepts.description: Repeating code with for and while, often over each item in a list.

concepts.name: Functions
concepts.description: Named reusable blocks of code that take inputs and may return a result.

concepts.name: Reading error messages
concepts.description: Interpreting tracebacks to find the line and type of a problem in a program.

misconceptions.description: Believes saving a file runs it automatically, but actually Python only runs code when you execute it.
Believes the text printed on screen is the program itself, but actually it is only the result of running the program.
Believes any text typed into a file is a valid program, but actually Python requires exact syntax to run.
Believes the = sign checks equality, but actually it assigns a value to a name.
Believes a variable can only hold the value it was first given, but actually reassigning replaces it.
Believes a variable keeps a link to the formula used to set it, but actually it stores only the computed value.
Believes '5' and 5 behave the same, but actually text and numbers are different types.
Believes decimal numbers are stored exactly, but actually floats can have small rounding errors.
Believes True is the word 'true' in quotes, but actually it is a boolean value.
Believes / always returns a whole number, but actually it returns a float result.
Believes Python evaluates operators strictly left to right, but actually multiplication and division come before addition and subtraction.
Believes + means addition for every type, but actually with strings it joins text.
Believes string methods modify the original text, but actually they return a new string.
Believes the first character is at index 1, but actually Python indexes start at 0.
Believes the quote marks are part of the stored text, but actually they only delimit it.
Believes assigning a list to a new name makes a separate copy, but actually both names refer to the same list.
Believes list positions begin at 1, but actually they begin at 0.
Believes append returns the updated list, but actually it changes the list and returns None.
Believes every branch of an if chain runs, but actually only the first true branch runs.
Believes = works for comparing values in an if, but actually comparisons use ==.
Believes else must have its own condition, but actually it runs when no earlier condition was true.
Believes the loop variable is a copy of the list, but actually it takes each item's value in turn.
Believes a while loop always runs at least once, but actually it checks the condition first.
Believes a loop stops by itself when the list is empty, but actually a while loop without a changing condition runs forever.
Believes writing a def line runs the function, but actually it only defines it until it is called.
Believes print sends a value back to the caller, but actually return does that and print only shows it.
Believes changing a parameter changes the caller's variable, but actually it changes only the local name.
Believes an error means Python is broken, but actually it reports a mistake in your code.
Believes the last line is always the cause, but actually the traceback shows the path to the failing line above it.
Believes changing random lines will fix an error, but actually the message points to where to look.

questions.prompt: You save a file named hello.py containing print('Hi') but never run it. What appears on screen?

options.text: Hi appears when the editor closes
Hi appears as soon as the file is saved
Nothing appears, because the code has not run
The line print('Hi') appears as text

questions.explanation: Python only runs code when you execute it, so saving the file alone produces no output.

questions.prompt: Which command runs a script saved as hello.py from a terminal?

options.text: Save hello.py again in the editor
Open hello.py in a text editor

questions.explanation: Running python followed by the file name tells the interpreter to execute the script.

questions.prompt: What is printed when you run a file containing print(2 + 3)?

options.text: Nothing, saving the file runs it

questions.explanation: The print call evaluates 2 + 3 and displays the result, which is 5.

questions.prompt: You change 'Bye' to 'Hi' in script.py, save it, but the terminal still shows Bye. What explains this?

options.text: Python reruns when the file name changes
The printed text is stored in the file, so Bye remains
Execute the script again to see the new output
Saving the file reruns the script in the background

questions.explanation: Terminal output is a result of a past run, so the script must be executed again to reflect the edit.

questions.prompt: Which file content will Python run without a syntax error?
questions.explanation: Statements separated by a semicolon are valid, while missing separators or stray words cause syntax errors.

questions.prompt: In a notebook cell containing print(3 + 4), you press run and see 7 below the cell. What is that 7?

options.text: The code itself, displayed as output
Text saved into the notebook file automatically
A copy of the cell made when you typed it
The result of running the code

questions.explanation: Running the cell executes print, and the 7 is the evaluated result shown after execution.

questions.prompt: A file contains Print("done") and was saved, but running it gives an error. What is the likely cause?

options.text: Saving the file should have run it again
The file is missing the output text
Python ignores capital letters in names
Python is case-sensitive; print is lowercase

questions.explanation: Python requires exact spelling, so Print is not recognized and must be written as print.

questions.prompt: What does the line total = 10 do?

options.text: Makes total fixed at 10 for good
Stores the value 10 under the name total

questions.explanation: The = sign assigns the value 10 to the name total. It does not compare or link anything.

questions.prompt: After a = 3 and then a = 7, what is a?

options.text: Error, since a cannot be assigned twice

questions.explanation: Assigning a new value replaces the old one, so a holds 7 afterwards.

questions.prompt: After x = 4, y = x, x = 9, what is y?

options.text: 9, because y stays linked to x

questions.explanation: y = x copies the value 4 into y at that moment. Changing x later does not change y.

questions.prompt: After price = 20, tax = price * 0.1, then price = 50, what is tax?

options.text: Error, because price was already set

questions.explanation: tax stored the computed value 2.0 when it was assigned. Later changes to price do not recalculate it.

questions.prompt: count = 0, then three times count = count + 1. What is count at the end?

options.text: 0, because count keeps its first value
4, since count + 1 is re-run as a formula

questions.explanation: Each pass reads the current value of count, adds 1, and assigns the result back. After three passes count is 3.

questions.prompt: name = Ana, greeting = Hi + name, name = Ben. What does print(greeting) show?

options.text: Hi Ben, since greeting tracks name
Hi name, since the text stays unevaluated

questions.explanation: greeting was built from the value of name at that time, which was Ana. Reassigning name later does not change greeting.

questions.prompt: score = 10, then the line score == 10 runs. What is score afterwards?

options.text: True, because the comparison overwrites score
Error, since == needs a second name
True, since score stays linked to 10 == 10

questions.explanation: == compares and produces True, but nothing is assigned to score. So score still holds 10.

questions.prompt: What does type('42') return?
questions.explanation: The quotes make '42' text, so its type is str, even though it looks like a number.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a boolean value?
questions.explanation: True without quotes is the boolean value; in quotes it is just text.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a float?
questions.explanation: 2.0 has a decimal point, so it is a float; 2 is an int and '2.0' is text.

questions.prompt: What does print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) display?
questions.explanation: Floats store binary approximations, so 0.1 + 0.2 is slightly above 0.3 and the comparison is False.

questions.prompt: name = input('Age: ') gives '21'. Which expression gives 29?
questions.explanation: input returns text, so it must be converted with int before adding the number 8.

questions.prompt: flag = 'False' is set, then 'if flag:' is run. What happens?

options.text: The block is skipped because the text says False
The block runs after converting to a number
The block runs; text is truthy
A TypeError is raised for text in an if

questions.explanation: Any non-empty string counts as true in a condition, so the block runs even though the text reads False.

questions.prompt: In a new script, what type is the value of 'cat' == 'dog'?
questions.explanation: Comparisons return a boolean value, here False, so the type is bool.

questions.prompt: What is the value of 1 + 6 / 2 in Python?
questions.explanation: Division runs before addition, so 6 / 2 gives 3.0 and then 1 + 3.0 gives 4.0.

questions.prompt: What does print('ab' + 'c') output?
questions.explanation: With strings, + joins the text in order, so 'ab' followed by 'c' gives 'abc'.

questions.prompt: What is the value of 10 / 4 in Python 3?
questions.explanation: The / operator performs true division and returns a float, so 10 / 4 is 2.5.

questions.prompt: What is the value of 2 + 3 * 4 - 6 / 2 in Python?
questions.explanation: Multiplication and division run first, giving 2 + 12 - 3.0, which is 11.0 because / returns a float.

questions.prompt: What does print('Ha' + 'Ha' * 2) output?
questions.explanation: The * operator runs first, so 'Ha' * 2 gives 'HaHa', and then 'Ha' + 'HaHa' joins to 'HaHaHa'.

questions.prompt: A teacher computes the average of three test scores with avg = (80 + 90 + 70) / 3. What value does avg hold?
questions.explanation: The parentheses group the sum to 240, and dividing by 3 with / gives the float 80.0.

questions.prompt: A shop computes total = 2 + 3 * 1.5. What value does total hold?
questions.explanation: Multiplication runs before addition, so 3 * 1.5 is 4.5 and adding 2 gives 6.5.

questions.prompt: s = "cat"; print(len(s))
questions.explanation: The length counts the three letters c, a and t; the quote marks only delimit the text and are not stored in it.

questions.prompt: word = "hi"; what does word[0] give?
questions.explanation: Python indexes start at 0, so index 0 is the first character, h.

questions.prompt: s = "dog"; t = s.upper(); print(s)
questions.explanation: upper() returns a new uppercase string and leaves s unchanged, so printing s shows the original lowercase text.

questions.prompt: s = "python"; print(s[1:4])
questions.explanation: Slicing from index 1 up to but not including index 4 takes the characters at indexes 1, 2 and 3, which are y, t and h.

questions.prompt: s = "data"; s.replace("a", "o"); print(s)
questions.explanation: replace() returns a new string with the substitution, but since its result is not assigned, s still holds the original text data.

questions.prompt: msg = 'say "hi"'; print(len(msg))
questions.explanation: The text say "hi" has 8 characters, including the space and the two double quotes that sit inside the string; the outer single quotes are only delimiters.

questions.prompt: word = "cat"; word2 = word.capitalize(); print(word, word2)
questions.explanation: capitalize() returns a new string, so word keeps its original value while word2 holds Cat.

questions.prompt:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
nums.append(40)
What is nums[3]?
questions.explanation: append adds 40 to the end, so the list is [10, 20, 30, 40] and index 3 holds 40.

questions.prompt: nums = [1, 2, 3]. What does nums.append(4) return?
questions.explanation: append changes the list in place and returns None, so assigning its result gives None.

questions.prompt: fruits = ["apple", "pear", "fig"]. Which expression gives "pear"?
questions.explanation: Positions start at 0, so "pear", the second item, is at index 1.

questions.prompt:
x = [1, 2, 3]
y = x
y[0] = 99
What is x now?
questions.explanation: y = x makes both names refer to the same list, so changing y[0] also changes x.

questions.prompt:
nums = [1, 2]
result = nums.append(3)
print(result[0])
What happens?

options.text: It prints 2 because positions start at 1
It prints [1, 2, 3] because append returns the list
It raises TypeError because result is None
It prints 1 because result holds the list

questions.explanation: append returns None, so result is None and indexing it raises TypeError.

questions.prompt:
def add_item(cart):
    cart.append("milk")
mycart = ["eggs"]
add_item(mycart)
print(mycart)
What is printed?
questions.explanation: The function receives the same list object, so append changes mycart itself.

questions.prompt:
letters = list('abc')
letters.insert(0, 'z')
What is letters[1]?
questions.explanation: After inserting 'z' at position 0, the list is ['z', 'a', 'b', 'c'], so index 1 holds 'a'.
The condition x > 3 is true, so the if branch runs and prints 'big'. The else branch is skipped.
x > 10 is false and x > 5 is true, so only the elif branch runs and prints 'B'. Once one branch runs, the rest are skipped.

questions.prompt: What does the else branch of an if statement do?

options.text: Runs when its own test is true
Runs when the if is false

questions.explanation: The else block runs when the preceding if condition evaluates to False. It has no condition of its own.
75 fails the first test but passes score >= 70, so the second branch runs. The remaining elif is skipped, so only 'B' prints.

questions.prompt: Which line correctly checks whether the variable name equals 'Ana'?
questions.explanation: In Python, == compares two values for equality inside a condition. A single = is assignment and is a syntax error in an if.

questions.prompt: A vending script has: if coins >= price: dispense(); elif coins > 0: show('more coins needed'); else: show('insert coins'). With coins = 0 and price = 1, what is shown?
questions.explanation: coins >= price and coins > 0 are both false, so the else branch runs and shows 'insert coins'. Only one branch runs in the chain.

questions.prompt: In a shop script, an if checks is_member and an else sets price to 10. When does the else block run?

options.text: Right after the if block runs

questions.explanation: The else block runs whenever the if condition is False, here when is_member is False. It needs no condition of its own.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?
nums = [1, 2, 3]
for n in nums:
    print(n)
questions.explanation: The for loop assigns each list item to n in turn, so each item is printed once and the loop then ends.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?
x = 5
while x < 3:
    print("hi")
questions.explanation: A while loop checks its condition before each pass, and 5 < 3 is False, so the body never runs.

options.text: a, b, c, then repeats forever
c, c, c on separate lines
a, b, c on separate lines

questions.explanation: The for loop takes each character of the string in order, so each one is printed on its own line.

questions.prompt:
This loop should print "go" three times but prints forever. What fixes it?
count = 0
while count < 3:
    print("go")

options.text: Move the print above the while line
Add count = count + 1 in the loop body
Add count = 0 above the while line

questions.explanation: A while loop needs its condition to change inside the body, so incrementing count lets it eventually become False.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?
ready = False
while ready:
    print("hello")
    ready = True
questions.explanation: The condition ready is False when the while line is first checked, so the body is skipped entirely.

questions.prompt:
A player has 2 lives and this loop runs:
lives = 2
while lives > 0:
    print("Still playing")
What happens?

options.text: It stops when the list is empty

questions.explanation: Nothing inside the loop changes lives, so the condition stays True and the loop never ends on its own.

questions.prompt:
A queue is empty when this runs:
queue = []
while queue:
    serve(queue.pop())
What happens?

options.text: An error is raised before the loop

questions.explanation: The while loop checks whether queue has items first, and an empty list is falsy, so serve is never called.
A def line only defines the function; its body runs only when the function is called.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of return inside a function?

options.text: Sends a value back to the caller

questions.explanation: return hands a value back to the code that called the function so it can be stored or used.

questions.prompt: Given def area(n): return n * n, which line correctly calls the function with 3?
questions.explanation: Calling a function means writing its name followed by the argument in parentheses.

questions.prompt:
def add_one(n):
    n = n + 1

x = 5
add_one(x)
print(x)

What is printed?
questions.explanation: Assigning n inside the function changes only the local name, so x still holds 5.

questions.prompt:
def double(n):
    print(n * 2)

result = double(4)
print(result)

What is printed, in order?
questions.explanation: print shows 8 but does not return it, so double returns None and result holds None.

questions.prompt:
def price(x):
    return x + 2

total = price(5) * 2
print(total)

What is printed?
questions.explanation: price(5) returns 7, which is then doubled to 14.

questions.prompt:
def score(p):
    p = p + 10
    return p

bonus = 3
score(bonus)
print(bonus)

What is printed?
questions.explanation: The returned value is discarded, and reassigning p inside score never changes bonus.

questions.prompt: Python shows NameError: name 'totl' is not defined, pointing to line 4. What does this mean?

options.text: Python's installation is damaged and needs reinstalling.
The error is on the last line of the file, so edit it there.
Random edits to any line should clear the NameError.
Line 4 uses a name 'totl' that Python cannot find in your code.

questions.explanation: The message names the problem (an undefined name 'totl') and the line where it is used, so the fix is in your code at that spot.

questions.prompt: A traceback lists File app.py line 10 in main, then File utils.py line 3 in parse, then ValueError. Where should you look first?

options.text: Edit app.py line 10 right away, since it is listed.
Line 3 of utils.py, where the error was raised.
Reinstall Python, since the traceback shows a crash.
The ValueError line at the bottom, since it is last.

questions.explanation: The traceback lists the path of calls, and the deepest frame, utils.py line 3, is where the exception was actually raised.

questions.prompt: Python prints a SyntaxError pointing at one line. What is the best first step?

options.text: Change lines at random until the error disappears.
Assume Python has a bug and try a different version.
Jump to the final line of the file and rewrite it.
Read the line shown and check it for a typo or missing symbol.

questions.explanation: A SyntaxError marks the place where Python could not parse your code, so checking that line for a mistake is the efficient first step.

questions.prompt: Traceback: File report.py line 9 in module calls average(scores); File report.py line 4 in average runs return total / count; then ZeroDivisionError. The list passed is empty. Which line should you inspect to fix the root cause?

options.text: Python's division code, since the interpreter is faulty.
Line 4, where count is zero for an empty list.
Random lines in report.py until the division stops failing.
The ZeroDivisionError line, since it is the last shown.

questions.explanation: The division on line 4 is where the exception is raised, and the empty list makes count zero there, so the root cause is visible at that line.

questions.prompt: A program prints KeyError: 'apples' at line 12, where stock['apples'] is used. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Python's dictionary feature is broken on this computer.
The last line of the file has the wrong dictionary name.
The dictionary stock has no key 'apples' when line 12 runs.
Changing the print on line 12 at random should add apples.

questions.explanation: KeyError names the missing key and line 12 is where the lookup fails, so the dictionary contents at that moment are the thing to check.

questions.prompt: In game.py, line 15 calls pick(), and the traceback shows IndexError: list index out of range raised at line 7 inside pick. Where is the fix most likely?

options.text: Line 15, the last line shown, since it is the final call.
Line 7 inside pick, where the bad index is used.
The Python installation, which needs repair.
Random lines in game.py until the IndexError goes away.

questions.explanation: The exception is raised at line 7 where the index is applied, so the fix belongs there or in the value that the caller passes in.

questions.prompt: A file gives SyntaxError: '(' was never closed, pointing at line 3, while line 8 looks fine. What does this suggest?

options.text: Edit any random line until the bracket message disappears.
The unclosed bracket starts on line 3, so the error is there.
Line 8 is the real problem, since it is the last code line.
Python is broken, so line 8 is correct as written.

questions.explanation: Python reports where the unclosed bracket began, so the missing closing symbol is near line 3 even though the parser fails later.
